This trigonal symmetry is crucial for the substance's key functions, which include acting as a desiccant, cooling agent, and reverse osmosis membrane filler. The study employs density functional theory calculations to examine the structural and electronic properties of ammonium sulfate in both its high- and low-temperature phases. Furthermore, phonon dispersion curves were generated to corroborate the stability of the predicted transition temperatures. The chemical stability of ammonium sulfate is attributed to these broad energy bands. This study presents an efficient approximation for the Fréchet distance, applicable to arbitrary polygonal curves, specifically targeting the scenario where one or both curves consist exclusively of straight line segments parallel to coordinate axes. These axis-aligned segments possess a minimum defined thickness, allowing their apparent zero width to be attributed to visual representation on a screen. Although general Fréchet distance computation is #P-hard, we present Algorithm 1, which approximates this value in quasi-linear time relative to the curve lengths, contingent on logarithmic complexity. This efficiency is achieved by leveraging the geometric constraints of the thickened curves, which geometrically broaden feasible flow rates within a network structure to substantially lower the underlying combinatorial hurdle. We further introduce Algorithm 2, another efficient method designed to detect similarity among these curves within a specified Fréchet tolerance.

Measurement Error Mitigation (MEM) refers to post-processing techniques designed to address persistent readout inaccuracies in quantum computing (QC). Current MEM strategies are largely developed for and tested on quantum computing architectures, yet they remain underexplored in the context of hybrid HQC-QC systems. In such architectures, classical bits first encode quantum input data, which is then stored in quantum memory. Consequently, errors can arise from the combined processes of data loading and persistent QC readout. This study examines a specific MEM method within these hybrid systems, demonstrating that it can either fully correct or significantly reduce cumulative errors from both loading and measurement stages. These findings offer a basis for future work on robust MEM protocols tailored to general hybrid HQC-QC systems.

Assisting users with everyday tasks, from preparing meals to operating household appliances, is a promising area for robotic research. To succeed in these scenarios, robots must accurately interpret how users manage controls on appliances. Understanding the broad categories of robotic assistance, specifically "assisted teleoperation," highlights a critical need: robots must also communicate their own chosen command management to users. Drawing from related work, this study introduces assistance strategies that enable robots to share learned control methods. First, emphasizing clarity, it is highlighted that user feedback on a robot's chosen set of commands is integral to this process. Subsequently, a demonstration is provided where the "Command and Duration" approach is utilized to teach a robot how to operate a microwave, highlighting the importance of defining clear command boundaries. Finally, an experiment is conducted to evaluate the effectiveness of the assistance approach and user reactions to it.

Autonomous navigation in unknown settings is a crucial capability for mobile robots, requiring the creation of real-time maps of their surroundings. This environment is frequently characterized as a complex, multi-dimensional optimization challenge. However, recent advancements have shown that employing deep learning to generate these maps simultaneously and estimate degrees of freedom can achieve a near-perfect balance of accuracy and computational efficiency. This approach effectively addresses most difficult real-world scenarios, such as searching and rescuing operations.

Furthermore, we introduce the development and evaluation of a specialized network architecture designed to produce topologically precise maps, which have been integrated into an autonomous navigation framework based on SLAM. The resulting robotic platform, equipped with this new technology, has been deployed in various real-world environments to assess its performance. Our findings indicate that the platform can successfully navigate even the most challenging unknown areas.

The emergence of the Internet of Things (IoT) has necessitated the development of next-generation wireless networks to connect a vast multitude of devices. A defining characteristic of these networks is the spatial distribution of users across two-dimensional planes, making the Two-Dimensional Multi-Dimensional MIMO (2D-MIMO) architecture—originally designed for line users in later-generation wireless systems—an ideal fit. Consequently, this paper investigates the application of 2D-MIMO within IoT scenarios. We begin by outlining the distinctive traits of IoT environments, such as the significant correlation among user channels and limited spatial separation. We then introduce a novel channel estimation method based on a low-rank approximation of channel matrices derived from a grid-based structure. Furthermore, our approach for user channel estimation incorporates feedback compression using singular value decomposition. Experimental results indicate that our scheme achieves performance comparable to state-of-the-art techniques while significantly reducing estimation overhead. Finally, we analyze the relationship between the overall system performance and the dimensions of the two-dimensional antenna array.

Computed Tomography (CT) has become a standard diagnostic tool in medicine, yet inaccuracies in beam attenuation coefficients can compromise image quality. While monochromatic X-rays eliminate attenuation artifacts, most clinical X-ray sources are polyenergetic, which can introduce artefacts like cupping and banding caused by variations in the effective energy of the beam as it traverses different path lengths. This study presents an algorithm designed to estimate the spectral distribution of polyenergetic X-ray sources by solving a system of linear equations derived from measured attenuation at various thicknesses. The accuracy of this proposed method is validated using both simulated and real-world data, specifically assessing the resulting spectral effective energy against the analytical values of monoenergetic X-rays. The calculated effective energy is then utilized to generate corrected projections, which significantly reduce artefacts in reconstructed CT images. Furthermore, the estimated spectral data enables more precise quantification of linear attenuation by accounting for the specific attenuation of individual X-ray photons.

This work investigates the propagation of light through and scattering from metallic areas with subwavelength dimensions. Utilizing a local response model to describe metal dielectric functions, absorbed energy and radiated light are analyzed via finite-difference time-domain (FDTD) simulations and analytical methods. We identify that local response models can cause calculated energy absorption to become infinite if the material's absorption coefficient diverges at a specific wavelength, even within very short distances. To resolve this unphysical outcome, we apply corrections to the local response framework. Additionally, we develop an analytical expression for light transmission and reflection in these narrow strips, a formula valid in both the quasi-static and non-diffraction regimes.

Although the benefits of integrating context into traditional retrieval models are well-documented, resolving the "sparsity of signals" challenge remains unresolved. We introduce CoRe, a collaborative retrieval framework that leverages feedback from multiple users to boost model performance. CoRe functions as a user-centric, distributed, and pre-trained system capable of effectively routing queries to similar users for context extraction. This pre-training phase empounds the system to discern relevant information within free-text chat contexts, drawing inspiration from the abundant data found in messaging applications. CoRe operates by first identifying users with shared interests during collaboration, a step we demonstrate is best achieved through manual selection of context containing keywords rather than relying on automated methods. Furthermore, the system facilitates this process by selecting these pre-trained terms specifically to foster user similarity groupings. Our empirical findings confirm that this pre-training strategy and human-driven collaborative context selection together substantially enhance recall within chat-based scenarios.

This paper addresses forecasting multivariate time series by examining diverse examples that exhibit anticipated features, such as seasonal patterns, multiple interdependencies, and non-stationarity. After evaluating conventional methods like ARIMA and AutoRegressve Moving Average models with Regressve Sliding windows, the study proposes integrating multiple predictors into an Ensemble Approach which leverages machine learning techniques including Random Forests and Gradient Boosting. Furthermore, multiple models are combined using weighted averaging to enhance performance on complex datasets like those found in finance, health, and engineering. The proposed Ensemble Approach outperforms individual models in terms of accuracy and robustness across a variety of scenarios. In conclusion, combining multiple models into an integrated framework provides superior results compared to single models when dealing with these challenging problems.

Machine learning algorithms applied to Electronic Health Records (EHRs) hold significant promise for enhancing healthcare quality and efficiency by addressing diverse medical challenges. However, error-prone data within EHRs can compromise the reliability of model outcomes, a flaw that is often magnified during data preprocessing. To address this, the current study proposes a two-tiered framework designed to cleanse and rectify misclassified EHR entries. Initially, a contextual analysis technique is employed to detect inconsistencies in clinical documentation. Subsequently, these issues are mitigated by leveraging transformer-based models for task-specific rectification. This methodology was validated using a multi-task benchmarking suite on the MIMIC-III dataset. The framework's efficacy was further demonstrated through its application to medical coding and the construction of an inconsistent, non-normalized EHR dataset to test its performance.

These influences arise from two primary sources: electrostatic interactions among ions in the immediate vicinity of surfaces, which are addressed through a linear or nonlinear Poisson-Boltzmann framework, and solvent polarization effects. The latter is calculated via a linear approximation of a Poisson equation specific to electrolytes, incorporating a dielectric constant that varies spatially. Automating the identification phase within requirements texts marks a crucial initial step toward automating requirements management. This study introduces a new approach to identify a requirements' effects by leveraging existing effects as guidance to streamline identification. Since applying this approach across all possible stored effects from a requirements repository is computationally expensive, the proposed model characterizes effects based on natural language word embeddings. By representing effects as continuous vector models, the approach achieves a significant reduction in computational costs while maintaining high accuracy. The new technique operates in two sequential stages: first, effects are selected from the repository using a vectorial similarity metric, and second, machine learning algorithms are utilized to identify specific impacts on entities and their connections. An empirical analysis was conducted to validate and assess this proposed model.

We first derive closed-form expressions for network coding-based EE, closing the gap in previous work. Next, we propose a practical method for determining the optimal fractional transmission power needed to maximize EE within an network coding framework. Furthermore, we offer a strategy to find EE-optimal EE values across fractional power settings. We then evaluate these findings by comparing them to scenarios involving traditional transmission schemes. Results indicate that the EE peak in network coding systems exceeds that of non-coding counterparts by up to 11.6% and shows superior scalability. By utilizing a superconducting quasiclassical surface-impurity theory, a comprehensive analytical framework for these scenarios is established. In addition to identifying inherent Yu-Shiba-Rusinov (YSR) bound states, our findings account for a broad spectral background. A novel differentiating characteristic is introduced to separate YSR states from the surrounding background. The analysis covers a comprehensive set of local exchange parameters and includes a comparative discussion with existing Yu-Shiba-Rusinov theories.

Distribution-to-distribution registration methods are extensively employed to align point clouds in static environments, yet they struggle significantly with dynamic scenes. In static contexts, these methods rely on the premise that point distributions share similar statistical properties, such as through point-to-point density measurements. Conversely, they fail in dynamic settings because they lack the capability to detect moving objects or apply appropriate constraints to exclude them from alignment. This research introduces a novel approach for distributing point cloud registration within dynamic contexts by integrating point features, which are computed from the point's local neighborhood geometry and self-color. Leveraging the characteristic that features remain constant across time steps for stationary objects, we perform distribution-based maximum likelihood estimation to find the optimal transformation that best fits these invariant features. Experimental results across both static and dynamic benchmarks demonstrate that this method surpasses current state-of-the-art techniques.

Satellite imagery is widely used across diverse sectors like agriculture, urban planning, and disaster relief monitoring. However, the sheer volume of imagery makes it difficult to identify specific events or changes. While recent methods relying on computer vision aim to improve this, they often lack the necessary robustness and accuracy. This paper introduces a new framework designed to generate reliable summaries of satellite images. By constructing a graph from image features and utilizing these graph structures for semantic segmentation, the proposed approach produces accurate and detailed summaries that capture image content. Testing on the SentinCity dataset, where image content must be summarized for a given query, demonstrates that this method surpasses current state-of-the-art performance. Additionally, to address the limitation of requiring labeled data for image feature creation, the method has been paired with semi-supervised learning techniques for pre-training, a process further strengthened by data augmentation. Finally, a user study was conducted to evaluate the subjective impact of these learned summaries on content understanding and search.

Non-linear X-ray Absorption Near Edge Spectroscopy (XANES) is a technique used to observe ionization-induced electronic changes within matter. However, interpreting these signals is difficult because response mechanisms vary across different timescales and X-ray fluences, and the resulting fluence-dependence in non-linear effects is not yet fully understood. In this work, we present a comprehensive study of non-linear XANES in CaF$_2$ and LiYF$_4$ across a wide range of incident fluences and photon energies. By combining experimental data with first-principles simulations, we demonstrate that changes in non-linear signals largely stem from changes in the effective cross-section for X-ray absorption rather than significant electron-hole recombination. Our findings indicate that effective absorption-coefficient shifts are primarily driven by high-energy photoelectrons, which are most effectively modeled by shifting the cross-section along the energy axis. Furthermore, by integrating measured shifting parameters with theoretical absorption-coefficient calculations from XANES and extended X-ray Fine Structure (XAFS) spectra, we derive reliable effective absorption-coefficient values. These coefficients, validated by comparisons with experimental ion yields, provide a robust quantitative basis for modeling the linear response to X-rays in materials.

Automatic modulation classification (AMC) is a critical component of cognitive radio systems, enabling receivers to identify the transmitted signal type. Over recent years, the application of Deep Neural Networks (DNN) to this task has demonstrated significant potential. However, designing a robust DNN for AMC involves selecting an optimal architecture, which is often difficult due to the broad range of possible configurations and the scarcity of research comparing different designs. This paper introduces a novel DNN-based equalizer that leverages the characteristics of both the transmitter and the communication channel to enhance the classification accuracy of various modulations. Extensive simulations across diverse signal-to-noise ratios (SNR) confirm that this proposed equalizer outperforms standard equalizers, surpassing accuracy levels by up to 15% under certain conditions.

Segmenting Multiple Sclerosis (MS) lesions in MRI images presents a significant challenge for both human radiologists and current deep learning models due to their highly variable appearance. While these data-intensive methods have traditionally required extensive labeled datasets, a recent shift has introduced knowledge distillation to transfer knowledge from underperforming models to highly accurate ones. However, a notable gap exists because no study has yet applied knowledge distillation specifically to MS lesion segmentation. In this study, we address this by improving a pre-trained, deep, unsupervised, self-attention U-Net for the MS segmentation task. To the best of our knowledge, this marks the first implementation of knowledge distillation within the domain of MS segmentation. Furthermore, we empirically evaluated various knowledge distillation approaches and implemented a new self-attention, multi-scale, U-shape architecture. The resulting model, called MoSeU-Net, consistently outperformed existing state-of-the-art techniques across multiple public datasets.

This work addresses the issue of learning dynamics systems modeled as ergodic, noise-free, continuous-time deterministic systems operating within fixed but unknown invariant measures. The study evaluates differential equation learners trained via snapshot data—measurements of state and state derivatives taken at random moments over training periods of duration T. As the learning algorithm refines its model with each new snapshot, $T$ represents the interval spanning the first to the final measurement. Under specific regularity conditions, the paper derives upper bounds for the generalization error in terms of both the number of snapshots and the time $T$. The analysis demonstrates that, as the snapshot count increases, the model's generalization error converges to that of a model trained exclusively on snapshot data from an infinitely long time interval. Furthermore, it is proven that for a standard model trained using data from an infinitely long time interval, the generalization error remains bounded with respect to the sample size. These theoretical findings are validated through simulations of simulated annealing processes.

We conducted millimeter-wave continuum observations of an infrared dark cloud (IDC) using the Atacama Millimeter Array, detecting a new substructure within a previously identified starless core. This substructure, characterized by a full width half maximum of approximately 0.21 arcseconds and a signal-to-noise ratio of 5.5, is attributed to a protostellar core. By comparing the mass of protostellar cores to their starless counterparts, we find their average ratio is 0.72, which is notably lower than the 1.44 average observed among prestellar cores in the molecular cloud. This discrepancy suggests that protostellar cores in the IDC are smaller, likely due to intense stellar winds and radiation from forming stars, which expel core material. This process may account for the scarcity of massive stars within these core populations.

Primordial black holes (PBHs) are hypothesized dark matter candidates that formed during the early universe due to the gravitational collapse of density fluctuations. This study employs Monte Carlo simulations to investigate PBHs as the source of an astrophysical gamma-ray signal detected by the High Energy Space Telescope (HESS). Specifically, we examine two scenarios: (1) the PBHs serving solely as dark matter, and (2) constituting a minority of dark matter alongside other unknown components. Our findings indicate that current or near-future gamma-ray detectors, including HESS, CTA, and LHAASO, can constrain or detect dark matter PBHs with masses within the range of $10^{25} - 10^{27}$ grams, provided their abundance is less than approximately 10% of the total dark matter density.

Simulations involved two-dimensional arrays of these molecules aligned in a rectangular box, with varying packing density controlled by the range [0.60, 0.40]. The system's structural behavior was analyzed across this density range, revealing a transition through liquid crystalline phases: at densities above 0.5, the molecules form a crystalline structure, while for densities below 0.5 they form nematic and smectic liquid crystals. The nematic and smetric phases were observed to coexist in an intermediate density range. The results indicate that these phases exhibit unique properties compared to other known materials, suggesting potential applications as advanced functional materials. Parameter-efficient tuning focuses on updating a restricted subset of parameters within large, pre-trained models while keeping the majority frozen. This approach reduces memory usage for training downstream tasks, allowing fine-tuning with fewer resources. In this work, I introduce a new strategy for selecting the parameters to update based on their sensitivity to gradients. By analyzing how critical each parameter is, the framework dynamically adjusts the size of these sensitive parameters throughout training, thereby enhancing their impact on the loss. Experiments indicate that this method matches the performance of standard full fine-tuning when used with equivalent small tuning layers.

This paper examines the ability of deep neural networks, specifically containing only one hidden layer, to equate two sets—denoted as $A$ and $B$—that become unequal following an add-one-element operation. Initially, when $|A| = |B|$, a straightforward difference-of-sums method (sum of $A$'s elements minus sum of $B$'s elements) suffices to achieve zero output. However, if an element is introduced, resolving this scenario with a single hidden layer is impossible. We propose instead to approximate this solution, interpreting this process as a task for the network to identify an appropriate "shift" that aligns the enlarged set back with its counterpart. Our analysis focuses on how network performance is affected by (i) the specific element added, (ii) the initial size of the original sets, and (iii) whether neural networks can effectively approximate these required "shifts."

This study establishes the interconnections between configurational enthalpy, internal energy, and entropy in polymer fluids. Unit tests are a critical component of modern software engineering, yet unit test defects remain a prevalent issue. Test smells, acting as proxies for unit test defects, signal the quality of the test code, yet existing research offers no guidance on whether the presence of these smells correlates with actual test effectiveness. This study addresses three specific research questions: (1) whether test smells can be used to predict failures in unit tests, (2) if such smells are linked to the effectiveness of unit tests, and (3) which specific smells serve as predictors for test failures. Data were collected from the Mozilla Suite, Mozilla Firefox, JUnit benchmark projects, and all available open-source unit test repositories on GitHub. Our findings indicate that certain test smells can indeed predict test failures and act as indicators of compromised effectiveness, offering developers a practical mechanism to identify and rectify issues to ensure the function of unit tests.

Heart-Beat Variability (HBV) is a metric that measures the time-based differences in the intervals between heartbeats, serving as a critical tool for diagnosing and tracking cardiovascular conditions. Manually recording HBV requires a specialist's involvement, which is laborious and costly. Conversely, HBV analysis can also be conducted automatically through electrocardiogram (ECG) signals. In this study, we present a novel convolutional neural network (CNN) model for classifying HBV directly from raw ECG data. Our approach eliminates the need for preprocessing steps such as signal filtering or beat detection, which are typically resource-intensive and error-prone. Instead, we utilize raw ECG data as the input for a CNN architecture composed of multiple convolutional and fully connected layers. The model's performance was evaluated on the HRV dataset within Physionet, specifically using leads from the V2, V3, and V4 views. Experimental outcomes indicate that this HBV classifier achieves an accuracy of 88.10% (85.21% precision, 85.21% recall, and an F1 score of 85.21%). Furthermore, we developed an additional HBV classifier based on the identification of QRS complexes. This model extracts inter-beat intervals from QRS detections to feed into a long short-term memory (LSTM) network. In this configuration, HRV detection reaches an accuracy of 84.21%

Achieving an efficient implementation of tensor singular value decomposition (t-SVD) is essential for effective tensor computation, yet its current format proves too verbose for efficient execution on data-parallel architectures characterized by numerous data streams. This analysis evaluates three space-optimized t-SVD formats, which are well-suited for modern hardware, with a specific focus on optimizing the centralized singular vector stage. This optimization leverages parallelism within the core matrix, enabling concurrent operations across multiple central singular vectors. Experimental results indicate that these parallel techniques yield significant throughput gains on both GPGPUs and many-core CPUs. Furthermore, these improvements facilitate the creation of space-efficient and rapid t-SVD libraries, which are applicable to a broad spectrum of tensor algorithms.

Dynamic graph embedding has become a standard method for representing time-evolving networks. It is frequently utilized to derive novel features for various applications, including link prediction, node classification, and graph sampling. However, current benchmarks typically evaluate only the methods themselves, often overlooking the reliability of features extracted as a critical component of these assessments. This paper introduces a framework designed to validate the reliability of features used in dynamic graph embeddings. We identify four specific failure modes that can cause features to be flawed: they may be a) non-discriminative, b) non-reproducible, c) non-categorical, or d) non-categorical in representing true underlying distributions. We also provide guidelines for addressing these issues to ensure features are suitable for specific tasks. Furthermore, we present a proposed framework for generating reproducible features and confirm the findings through an experimental analysis of three widely adopted dynamic graph embedding models.

Deep Metric Learning seeks to construct an effective feature space where similar items are closely grouped and distinct items are pushed apart, a process often termed learning a metric. Although these algorithms have achieved significant success in tasks like person re-identification and facial recognition, they are constrained by the need for large amounts of labeled pairs, a requirement impractical for many applications. Conversely, unsupervised pseudo-labeling strategies can mitigate this limitation by generating labeled pairs automatically, though they frequently fail to produce a dense and well-ordered feature map due to the sparsity of assigned labels. To address this, we introduce a new approach that learns a low-density feature space devoid of any prior label information. A core component of this method is a newly developed pair-wise loss function designed to maximize the count of under-utilized constraints within an unlabeled dataset, thereby driving more effective feature learning than its predecessors. Furthermore, we incorporate a clustering algorithm capable of operating during inference on unseen data to facilitate efficient integration with existing deep learning metrics and unsupervised loss functions.

Determining camera poses is fundamental to vision-based robot control, with established methods relying on feature matching or optical flow to achieve this. However, in scenarios where these approaches become unfeasible due to the total absence of visual features, estimating poses directly from image intensity distributions is necessary. This study introduces a range of both traditional current and state-of-the-art techniques that utilize neural networks for this specific task.

In many real-world scenarios, agents must learn from demonstrated examples while respecting specific constraints. This paper introduces a new approach for inference in such environments. By leveraging the fact that constraints are typically rigid and discrete, our method transforms them into a set of binary state variables. These variables are then used to generate constraint-aware state representations and to direct the sampling process during training. Consequently, agents can learn to respect constraints without ever violating them or encountering undefined regions. Extensive experiments demonstrate that these agents achieve higher rewards and exhibit greater behavioral diversity compared to current state-of-the-art approaches.

The GAIA mission of the European Space Agency is a space-based mission dedicated to mapping the entire galaxy with unprecedented precision through the observation of over a billion stars. The project, a major international collaboration, includes a data processing pipeline known as DDP that handles all information gathered from the telescope and combines it into the final science catalog. The pipeline consists of several software modules, each responsible for a specific task in the processing workflow. The pipeline's final module, DDP3 produces the last DDP2 product by cross-matching it with the final product from the module DDP1. The paper describes the algorithm of the matching algorithm used in the module DDP3, analyzes how the module handles errors in data, and investigates how the module can produce the most accurate list of cross matched products.

We present an algorithm for the full-family vertex separator problem applicable to a graph $G$ with $n$ vertices and a $k$-separator $S$. Our approach extends an existing strategy by Demaine et al., specifically by incorporating a novel technique to decrease the size of every separator in the computed family, thereby allowing larger time constants.

Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs), which embed physical laws into data-driven architectures, have achieved notable success. This paper introduces a framework for constructing robust and generalizable PINNs through a mapping pipeline of stacked, sequential networks. In a first network, observational data is mapped to a latent space defined by its adherence to physical laws. A second network then translates these latent representations into predictions in the observation space. By decoupling the observation mapping from the underlying physics, this approach yields robust and generalizable PINNs. Furthermore, this multi-stage structure facilitates easy parallelization across diverse scientific domains.

In the United States, respiratory and cardiovascular diseases are primary causes of illness and death, driven largely by air pollution. In epidemiological research, developing precise exposure models for these pollutants is essential for accurate analysis. This study evaluates a modeling approach that leverages machine learning and satellite imagery to generate refined estimates of air pollution, aiming to align with individual data points within specific geographic regions. The methodology utilizes spatial-temporal convolutional and recurrent neural networks to process satellite-derived information, generating preliminary pollution estimates. These serve as covariates within an iterative, expectation-maximization framework designed to fine-tune predictions, incorporating them alongside ground-based sensor readings. The research presents results from applications of this method across two regions: New York City and the Los Angeles Basin. The proposed technique demonstrates reduced error rates compared to standard satellite-only models, thereby offering more reliable exposure estimates that are particularly beneficial for studies examining the health impacts of air pollution.

These results confirm the robust detection of the peak in the total tunneling conductivity rather than just its derivative (differentiated response), suggesting a significant potential for the observation of topological features at much lower energy scales.

Adversarial Machine Learning is a rapidly evolving field that investigates model security, focusing on vulnerabilities to adversarial attacks. While significant research has historically centered on adversarial examples within the image domain, Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) are increasingly popular due to their ability to model complex relational data. Consequently, developing similar adversarial examples for Graph Classification and exploring their construction methods represents an emerging and novel area of study. This paper provides a concise overview of the current state of the art regarding Graph Neural Network security, specifically addressing adversarial examples tailored to graph classification. Furthermore, the paper outlines potential future research avenues within the domain of Adversarial Machine Learning.

Photometric catalogues are essential tools for investigating the large-scale structure of the sky; consequently, cross-matching sources between different entities is a fundamental prerequisite for inter-catalogue analysis. The primary difficulty in cross-matching arises from the fact that sources are often identified independently in each system, resulting in differing source identifiers, names, or magnitudes. Furthermore, existing algorithms typically rely on magnitude alone, failing to account for the varying photometric bands or filters used across catalogues. To address these limitations, we have developed a new cross-matching algorithm capable of comparing photometric catalogsues by utilizing bandpass information in addition to magnitude data. We have applied this method to create a joint sample of the SDSS DR16 and 2MASS catalogs, which includes over 1.5 billion cross-matches. This sample will serve as the foundation for upcoming studies on large-scale structure and galaxy evolution that leverage data from both sources.

A set $C$ constitutes a vertex cover for a hypergraph $\mathcal{H}=(\mathcal{Q}, \mathcal{E})$ when every edge in $\mathcal{H}$ contains at least one vertex from $C$. We term a vertex cover "minimal" if no edge is completely uncovered by any of its elements; in other words, removing any single element from $C$ would leave at least one edge untouched. This study examines the problem of randomly selecting a minimal vertex cover. We provide a characterization of the pure $r$-uniform $\mathcal{H}$-process—a continuous-time Markov chain that traces the evolution of a pure $r$-uniform random vertex cover—as a solution to a specific differential equation. This finding enables a complete description of the "gap" phenomenon associated with the 2-critical threshold. Finally, we present supporting numerical data to validate our findings and address potential conjectures.

Ontologies, which formalize structured sets of concepts and their interconnections, are increasingly vital in biomedicine. As these definitions grow more extensive and intricate, maintaining consistency and avoiding contradictions within the concept set becomes challenging. While ontology editors offer some validation tools, their capabilities are limited. Consequently, this paper introduces a novel approach that leverages the power of neural networks for ontology reasoning. We present the prototype system BrainRule, capable of automatically identifying logical contradictions based solely on an ontology's tableau. Experimental results indicate that this method surpasses existing techniques in terms of both speed and performance. Furthermore, we discuss the potential for adapting BrainRule's neural architecture to accommodate common limitations in ontology processing, such as handling large-scale datasets and processing input provided through natural language.

This paper introduces an innovative framework for learning a semi-supervised, cross-domain, differentiable attention model for automatic speech recognition (ASR) using CycleGAN. The proposed approach leverages an unsupervised, semi-supervised technique to handle the challenges of domain shifts in speech processing. It integrates CycleGAN with inter-domain losses to create a unified loss function, thereby narrowing the distributional disparity between datasets. The framework further features a shared, trainable decoder for ASR, supervised by the source domain and guided by pseudo labels generated from the target domain. The paper further details the formulation of the semi-supervised objective function by combining CycleGAN and the attention model's inter-domain losses. The framework's efficacy is evaluated on the English-Spanish MSASR and the German-English-ASR tasks, demonstrating that it outperforms the standard supervised method by 9.89% and 9.89%, respectively.

Active inference serves as a computational framework that elucidates how biological agents perceive and interact with their surroundings. Fundamentally a model-based approach to active inference, it posits that to function effectively, an agent must construct a probabilistic model of the world. Consequently, an agent's sensory experience and behavioral outputs are jointly explained by its top-down model and the actual state of reality. By integrating these two layers, active inference proposes a principled method for navigating an agent through a complex, partially observable environment. This paradigm is highly adaptable, capable of addressing a broad range of challenges in perception, action, and learning. This dissertation elucidates the underlying mathematical principles and adaptive learning mechanisms of active inference, presenting both theoretical advancements and practical demonstrations.

This study examines the thermodynamic stability of binary dimer-monomomer mixtures, leveraging dimer and monomer densities as independent order parameters. Utilizing the self-consistent mean-field framework, we derived an effective free energy functional and calculated the critical points of both the lower and upper critical points (UCP and LCP) within the framework of extended phase diagrams. Furthermore, the calculation incorporates the temperature-dependent structure factor to account for short-range correlations. Our findings confirm that dimer-monomomer mixtures exhibit Soret effect behavior. Additionally, the calculated phase diagrams are consistent with the experimental data obtained for the C$_{16}$H$_{35}$PO$_4$--C$_{16}$H$_{33}O$_7$ system.

Automated Essay Scoring (AES) demands a nuanced grasp of language to accurately automate the evaluation of student writings. Although various NLP advancements have enhanced AES capabilities, a critical deficiency remains: most evaluation metrics prioritize short-term memory, causing models to neglect long-term dependencies within the text. This study proposes a new metric to quantify such dependencies, facilitating their integration into AES models to boost performance and alignment with human evaluations. Furthermore, these models are designed to mitigate the effects of advanced writing skills that may mask the true quality of a student's essay.

Adaptive detection for pedestrians is crucial for diverse applications, yet the heterogeneity in data collection methods and environmental conditions across domains often leads to significant accuracy drops. This study introduces a novel framework for adapting to mixed domains specifically for the pedestrian detection task. This approach centers on localizing and classifying pedestrians while accounting for the variability of backgrounds across domains. The method employs two specialized modules: a domain-specific feature alignment component and a classification component. The feature alignment component reduces cross-domain discrepancies by integrating local feature embeddings with spatial contextual information to perform domain adaptation at the feature level. The classification component then addresses these inconsistencies through robust, distribution-invariant feature representations and domain-generalizable spatial patterns, ultimately enhancing detection precision. Extensive experiments on the newly created CADC dataset confirm its superiority over current state-of-the-art methods by demonstrating significant improvements in detection accuracy.

The widespread adoption of mobile devices has facilitated the amateur recording of music with consumer-grade equipment. However, recordings made with mass-market recording apps often suffer from distortions, including room acoustical reflections and noise. Although recent studies have addressed the removal of room reflections, limitations remain in effectively handling recordings contaminated by both reflections and simultaneous noise, particularly when a dry reference is absent. To address this, our study introduces a novel approach for isolating dry signals from music tracks affected by room reflections, a reference noise, and unknown noise without requiring a clean reference signal or a specific target model. The core method involves variational inference applied to a complex probabilistic framework featuring multiple latent variables. The parameters are estimated using the Expectation-Maximization algorithm, and the final time-frequency mask is derived from the posterior probability of the noise components. Experimental results indicate that our approach effectively estimates time-frequency masks, thereby enhancing the performance of subsequent tasks such as noise reduction and acoustic echo cancellation.

This study investigates the potential for detecting throwing errors in a virtual overarm throwing task utilizing the elbow joint's Point of Release (PoR), derived from the trajectories of the throwing arm. The research addresses two main inquiries: first, whether PoR errors can reliably identify mistakes, and second, if so, whether the timing of release relative to the ball's position influences PoR accuracy. Experiments involved 100 overarm attempts executed by 18 right-handed participants using a robot-arm haptic interface, with 40 of these intentionally executed as error throws. The results demonstrate that overarm throwing can indeed be successfully regulated through PoS analysis, as the release time significantly impacts PoS accuracy. Specifically, releasing the robotic arm either too early or too late generates substantial PoS deviations, even during flawless executions. Conversely, optimal release positioned at the deepest depth of the arc's trajectory yields minimal PoS variance. Furthermore, PoS effectively distinguishes between error and non-error throws when the release occurs prematurely or late, but proves ineffective if executed mid-throw. These observations suggest that the theoretical points of inflection on the ballistic trajectory are suboptimal release points. Instead, experimental releases positioned at the trajectory's lowest height proved most capable of revealing error throws.

Achieving robust Neural Machine Translation (MNT) hinges on effectively capturing the syntactic structures of sentences. This study investigates two approaches to integrating dependency and constituency parsing within MMT frameworks. Our proposed method involves adapting the recently introduced dependency-based framework to align with constituency parsing by deriving a dependency representation from the constituent structure. Specifically, we generate dependencies between nodes in a recursive neural network (RNN) constituency parse, guided by prediction mechanisms typical of dependency parsers. Results indicate that constituency parsing outperforms standard dependency parsing, particularly when the derived dependencies utilize structures formed by specific recursive RNN configurations. Furthermore, dependencies generated through this approach, along with their corresponding constituency input structures, surpass those obtained from traditional word-sequence models using both bidirectional LSTMs and attention mechanisms, yielding the highest translation accuracy. To enable a language-capturing model to output text in varied styles—ranging from factual to emotional—this study proposes a conditional style-style language-capturing framework. This approach incorporates a separate encoder that converts textual style descriptors into conditional vectors, guiding the generation process. The proposed method utilizes pre-trained multi-label classifiers to assign style scores to images, which then inform the conditioning signals for a language-capturing model. The entire architecture is trained end-to-end to produce captions matching the specified nuances. This method demonstrates the ability to accurately capture specific stylistic elements and is further evaluated on a newly developed food-capturing dataset featuring diverse textual styles. Furthermore, this research demonstrates that conditional multi-label models can be effectively integrated into generation tasks, with extensibility shown via a dataset capable of handling over a hundred style categories.

The proliferation of autonomous systems and decision-making algorithms has placed harm caused by these technologies at the forefront of ethical analysis within this domain. However, existing frameworks for defining harm are predominantly grounded in traditional medicine, often overlooking the critical role of causation. Given that defining harm is inextricably linked to establishing causality, we examine how to apply a suitable causal model for defining harm in ethically analyzing algorithms and systems. We begin by outlining the key attributes that an effective causal model for defining harm must possess. Subsequently, we evaluate several established causal frameworks for their ability to address these criteria. Our findings suggest that current causal models are insufficiently robust to advance the ethical analysis of algorithms and systems. We acknowledge the challenges in developing new causal models and identifying appropriate methodologies. We hope to facilitate future research on defining harm by providing this foundational analysis, which may clarify the specific attributes any viable causal model for this purpose should incorporate.

To maximize the performance of both integrated components, a series of both generic and specialized execution strategies for deep learning tasks were engineered and evaluated. Testing, conducted on MNN coupled with Apache Flink against these benchmarks, demonstrated that our integrated system outperforms the existing approaches in terms of comprehensive execution efficiency and computational performance.

This work introduces a novel theory of dynamic boundary heat conduction based on the coupling of a Laplace layer model with a thermal bulk model, extending the interior approach originally proposed by Laplace. Within this framework, dynamic boundary temperature and heat flux are treated as independent variables. Historically, the Fourier–Planck model has relied on the assumption that surface temperature instantaneously matches the boundary temperature. This restrictive premise fails to represent real-world scenarios where a thermal lag exists between the boundary temperature and the actual local temperature at the material interface. By adopting this relaxed condition where temperature at the boundary need not equate to the local point temperature, the resulting dynamics align more closely with physical reality. This paper further demonstrates that the proposed dynamic boundary model can be derived directly from extensive thermodynamics principles using the balance of entropy. Additionally, stable static solutions to the governing equations were computed using the Newton method.

Accurate forecasting energy consumption holds significant value for numerous stakeholders. While predicting trends based on aggregated data across regions or companies is well-established, forecasting consumption specifically for individual customers is far more difficult due to high noise levels and a lack of clear patterns inherent in such data. This study addresses these challenges by designing a novel graph-based deep learning model designed to capture both temporal dynamics and structural relationships within the data. Additionally, it explores various strategies for constructing temporal graphs to determine their effectiveness in this context. The proposed approach demonstrates superior performance compared to leading models, yielding significant improvements in prediction accuracy—up to 10.3% for individual customer energy forecasts, a notable increase over the smaller 3.3% improvement achieved for aggregated predictions in the San Diego Load Profile dataset. The code implementing this work is available at https://github.com/robertkrajewski/GRU-D-Light-GCN.

Recent advancements in machine learning have yielded impressive results, yet significant obstacles remain in applying these techniques to real-world scenarios, notably regarding how to incorporate knowledge into models. Existing approaches to knowledge integration largely fall into two categories: logical rules and knowledge graphs. Although logical rules offer a structured way to embed knowledge via if-then statements, they struggle to capture complex relationships across diverse domains. Conversely, knowledge graphs facilitate multi-domain connections and query-based knowledge extraction; however, merging machine learning models with knowledge graphs is challenging, often necessitating the modification of pre-trained models to incorporate graph information. This review article offers a critical overview of state-of-the-art methods for knowledge graph embedding, focusing on how these technologies enhance machine learning models.

Despite the significant volume of training data available, current supervised segmentation approaches for analyzing chest CT images face challenges with blurry and irregular boundaries, often leading to unsatisfactory outcomes. To address these limitations, this paper introduces a new technique for post-processing segmentation maps derived from these inputs. The method employs a conditional generative adversarial network (cGAN) designed to correct boundary defects in initial segmentation results. The model's generator utilizes attention mechanisms alongside encoder-decoder structures to ensure precise localization of virus lesions without compromising internal details. Additionally, the defined discriminator focuses exclusively on assessing segmentation boundaries, which enhances the overall training efficiency. Experimental evaluations on two distinct COVID-19 chest-CT segmentation datasets confirm that this proposed method substantially improves boundary accuracy.

Precise localization and identification of vertebrae are essential for various clinical tasks, including diagnosing spinal diseases, screening for tumors, and planning surgeries. However, this process is often hindered by common pathologies such as scoliosis, which complicate the process. This paper introduces a new, challenging benchmark that features severe scoliosis to rigorously evaluate state-of-the-art methods. We address this challenge using a dual-task deep neural network approach, which simultaneously performs the tasks of localization and identification. The resulting deep learning models are trained using an end-to-end multi-task framework. We also establish and analyze the performance of several specialized methods for this specific challenge. The proposed solution achieves an overall accuracy of 96.8% for localization and 93.9% for identification, demonstrating that the current challenge represents the strictest test to date for these tasks.

The widespread adoption of next-generation home Wi-Fi networks is essential for delivering high-bandwidth applications, such as video on demand and cloud gaming, which rely on services like virtual reality and augmented reality. These applications demand extremely high data rates, low latency, and consistent quality, requirements that traditional access points (APs) alone cannot meet. To address this, researchers have proposed using software-defined networking (SDN) to create intelligent networks that adapt to user needs. This paper introduces a novel, SDN-driven solution designed to optimize performance in multi-user scenarios involving several access points. The approach first establishes a comprehensive mathematical model of a home environment, accounting for various factors including potential interference and signal attenuation. Subsequently, it defines a specific optimization problem aimed at maximizing network performance by determining the ideal placement and quantity of access points. Finally, the study introduces an efficient algorithm capable of solving this problem quickly, even when dealing with large-scale networks.
